# Promoting diversity in neurosurgery through a virtual symposium

**Authors:** Antoinette J. Charles; Andreas Seas; Jacquelyn Corley; Julia B. Duvall; Edwin Owolo; Nancy Abu-Bonsrah; Aladine A. Elsamadicy; Venita Simpson; Olabisi Sanusi; Langston T. Holly; Analiz Rodriguez; Edjah K. Nduom; Allan D. Levi; Linda M. Liau; Alfredo Quiñones-Hinojosa; Isaac Karikari; Gerald Grant; Anthony T. Fuller; C. Rory Goodwin

**Affiliations:** 1Equity and Justice in Neurosurgery, Durham | 2Department of Neurosurgery, Duke University, Durham | 3Pratt School of Engineering, Duke University, Durham, North Carolina | 4Harvard Medical School, Boston, Massachusetts | 5Department of Neurosurgery, Johns Hopkins School of Medicine, Baltimore, Maryland | 6Department of Neurosurgery, Yale School of Medicine, New Haven, Connecticut | 7Department of Neurosurgery, Baylor College of Medicine, Houston, Texas | 8Department of Neurosurgery, Oregon Health & Science University, Portland, Oregon | 9Department of Neurosurgery, David Geffen School of Medicine, University of California, Los Angeles, California | 10Department of Neurosurgery, University of Arkansas for Medical Sciences, Little Rock, Arkansas | 11Department of Neurosurgery, Emory University School of Medicine, Atlanta, Georgia | 12Department of Neurosurgery, University of Miami Miller School of Medicine, Miami | 13Department of Neurosurgery, Mayo Clinic, Jacksonville, Florida

## Abstract

The rates of women and underrepresented racial and ethnic minority (UREM) students successfully matching into neurosurgical residency are extremely low and do not reflect the makeup of the general population. As of 2019, only 17.5% of neurosurgical residents in the United States were women, 4.95% were Black or African American, and 7.2% were Hispanic or Latinx. Earlier recruitment of UREM students will help to diversify the neurosurgical workforce. Therefore, the authors developed a virtual educational event for undergraduate students entitled “Future Leaders in Neurosurgery Symposium for Underrepresented Students” (FLNSUS). The primary objectives of the FLNSUS were to expose attendees to 1) neurosurgeons from diverse gender, racial, and ethnic backgrounds; 2) neurosurgical research; 3) opportunities for neurosurgical mentorship; and 4) information about life as a neurosurgeon. The authors hypothesized that the FLNSUS would increase student self-confidence, provide exposure to the specialty, and reduce perceived barriers to a neurosurgical career.

To measure the change in participant perceptions of neurosurgery, pre- and postsymposium surveys were administered to attendees. Of the 269 participants who completed the presymposium survey, 250 participated in the virtual event and 124 completed the postsymposium survey. Paired pre- and postsurvey responses were used for analysis, yielding a response rate of 46%. To assess the impact of participant perceptions of neurosurgery as a field, pre- and postsurvey responses to questions were compared. The change in response was analyzed, and a nonparametric sign test was performed to check for significant differences.

According to the sign test, applicants showed increased familiarity with the field (p < 0.001), increased confidence in their abilities to become neurosurgeons (p = 0.014), and increased exposure to neurosurgeons from diverse gender, racial, and ethnic backgrounds (p < 0.001 for all categories).

These results reflect a significant improvement in student perceptions of neurosurgery and suggest that symposiums like the FLNSUS may promote further diversification of the field. The authors anticipate that events promoting diversity in neurosurgery will lead to a more equitable workforce that will ultimately translate to enhanced research productivity, cultural humility, and patient-centered care in neurosurgery.

In 2020, the Black Lives Matter social justice movement led many universities and medical centers around the country to examine their practices and begin more intentionally working toward building an equitable and antiracist environment. This movement propelled the call to action for racial and ethnic diversity in neurosurgery. Although there has been a rise in women trainees in neurosurgical residency programs, there has not been a commensurate increase in the number of Black, Hispanic, and Native American trainees.1 Neurosurgical trainees should ideally reflect their patient population to promote equitable care.2 Scientific reviews have demonstrated that establishing a racially diverse workforce improves patient satisfaction3 and treatment outcomes4 and enhances research productivity.5

Improving workforce diversity has been validated through pathway programs, longitudinal mentorship, and holistic medical school admissions reviews. Pathway programs provide exposure to careers in medicine and professional development opportunities for minority students and influence student preparedness to excel in academics.6 Longitudinal mentorship opportunities promote student retention in science, technology, engineering, and medicine fields, which will ultimately diversify the future applicant pool of medical students and residents.7 Moreover, these relationships also provide a sense of fulfillment to mentors, who feel a greater sense of personal gratification, productivity, and career satisfaction.8

One avenue to improve the representation of minorities in neurosurgery is to increase the pool of underrepresented racial and ethnic minority (UREM) students gaining acceptance to medical school. Although the number of matriculants overall has increased by over 20% during the past 15 years, there continues to be a decrease in the matriculation of Black, Hispanic, and Native American applicants.9 Adopting a more holistic review of applications through the consideration of leadership, research, and community engagement rather than test scores alone serves as an effective intervention to improve diversity.10 Notably, the establishment of the American Society of Black Neurosurgeons and the development of other neurosurgery-based affinity groups have also helped recruit UREM students to the field through targeted initiatives.11

With the advancements of technology and amplification of virtual learning experiences, we assembled a diverse team of leaders in neurosurgery. Together we developed a virtual neurosurgical educational event for undergraduate students entitled “Future Leaders in Neurosurgery Symposium for Underrepresented Students” (FLNSUS). The aim of the FLNSUS was to expose students to the tripartite mission of academic neurosurgery (research, education, and clinical care), educate them on life as a neurosurgeon, and connect them to current neurosurgeons from diverse backgrounds. We hypothesized that the FLNSUS would increase student self-confidence, provide exposure to the specialty, and reduce perceived barriers to pursuing a neurosurgical career.

## Methods

The FLNSUS was a 7-hour symposium held virtually on Saturday, August 7, 2021. The target audience was college-level students who identified as African American or Black, Hispanic or Latinx American, and Native American. We recruited participants through a social media campaign, partnerships with prehealth directors and advisors of historically black colleges and universities,12 and public universities with high student populations of Hispanic and Latinx Americans,13 Native Americans,14 and/or a low socioeconomic status.15

### Program Structure

The symposium had three components: introducing the career of neurosurgery, exposure to research, and building professional relationships between participants and role models at several stages, from medical students to residents to attending neurosurgeons. There were six interactive sessions: How to Become a Neurosurgeon, Cool Neurosurgical Cases, Career Panel, Tour of an Operating Room, Neurosurgery Research Panel, and Small Group Mentorship. The gender breakdown of the faculty guest speakers consisted of 4 women and 6 men. Six of the 10 neurosurgeons self-identified as African American or Black. Ethnically, 2 neurosurgeons self-identified as Hispanic or Latinx.

The session How to Become a Neurosurgeon explained the significant career milestones needed to pursue neurosurgery. The Career Panel was an opportunity for practicing neurosurgeons to inspire students with their personal experiences, insight, and passion for medicine. The Neurosurgery Research Panel exposed students to an overview of different neurosurgical research subspecialty areas and emphasized the importance of research. The Small Group Mentorship session allowed students to network and ask questions of faculty members, residents, and medical students.

### Survey Design

Ethical approval to assess the impact of the FLNSUS on participants for this study was granted by the institutional review board. To measure the change in participant perceptions surrounding neurosurgery, we administered pre- and postsymposium surveys to all attendees (Appendices A and B). Participants provided consent before filling out the surveys and attending the symposium. Responses were encoded with a unique identifying number to ensure confidentiality. A pretest survey was sent before the symposium launch, and completion was required to obtain the symposium login information. The posttest survey was sent to students immediately after the program’s conclusion. All students were awarded with a participation certificate without any monetary compensation. Students who completed the postsymposium survey received an invitation to apply for the Future Neurosurgeons Scholarship to help with Medical College Admission Test (MCAT) preparation and expenses associated with applying for medical school.

The answers to survey questions included multiple choice responses, Likert scale responses, and free-text responses. To enhance the study’s validity, questions were adapted from standardized surveys and questionnaires from published scientific studies.16–18 Demographic information in the presurvey included name, age, race, ethnicity, gender, sexual orientation, educational status, grade point average (GPA), parental/guardian education, family income, size of hometown (urban, suburban, rural), residential location (city, state), and family connection to physicians. The surveys also assessed career ambitions, knowledge and attractiveness of neurosurgery, involvement in research, and perceived barriers to becoming a neurosurgeon. To evaluate the impact of participant perceptions of neurosurgery as a field, responses to these questions were compared. To evaluate participant interest in FLNSUS-sponsored opportunities, we included questions in the postsurvey to indicate interest in applying to a longitudinal mentorship program and the Future Neurosurgeons Scholarship.

### Statistical Analysis

Several statistical methods were utilized to identify the impact of the symposium on student attendees. This impact was measured along three main axes: student interest in and understanding of a career in neurosurgery, student perceptions of minority representation in the field of neurosurgery, and perceived preparedness for a career in neurosurgery. Each of these areas was linked to Likert scale questions within the survey questionnaire (Appendices A and B).

To assess more granular changes in participant attitudes toward neurosurgery, we investigated their response to several key questions on a Likert scale (see Appendices A and B for pre- and postsurvey questionnaires, respectively). To check for significant changes in Likert responses, the difference between individual pre- and postsurvey scores was computed, and a sign test was performed on each specific question. To find group-specific trends, an N-Way ANOVA was performed on these Likert changes, considering several elements of individual identity.19 Any significant group-specific variability was subsequently assessed via chi-square test. A p value < 0.05 was used as the cutoff for statistical significance for all analyses.

All analyses were performed using Microsoft Excel and custom-built programs in MATLAB R2021a.

## Results

### Participant Student Demographics and Minority Identification

Participants in the first-ever FLNSUS came from a broad range of backgrounds and were at various stages of their training. A total of 269 students from all over the globe participated in FLNSUS 2021 (Fig. 1). Of the 269 participants who filled out the presymposium survey, 250 actually participated in the event and 124 ultimately completed the postsymposium survey. For our analyses, we utilized data from the 124 completed pre- and postsurvey student responses, although chi-square analysis of pre- and postsurvey demographics showed no significant difference between these populations (Appendix C).

Most participants identified as Black or African American (51.6%), with several students identifying as multiracial (8.9%). Approximately 30.6% of students identified as Hispanic or Latinx. Over 70% of participants identified as female, and slightly more than 10% of students identified as members of the lesbian, gay, bisexual, transexual, queer or questioning, etc. (LGBTQ+) community. Students ranged from high school sophomores to college graduates (Fig. 2).

### Measures of Symposium Impact

Symposium impact was measured through a range of questions on the pre- and postsurvey. When asked to rate the symposium, participants gave an average score of 9.46 out of 10 (95% CI 9.31–9.61). Students appeared to be excited by the symposium, with 98.4% indicating that they would attend a future symposium and 99.2% indicating that they would recommend the event to a family member, friend, or colleague. Two participant responses stand out as clear indications of the impact of this work.

Participant X: “There are less than 50 black women neurosurgeons in the country, and while I am extremely shocked to hear such a specific amount for the first time, I know I will be adding to that number.

Participant Y: “As a young Latina woman I find a lot of truth in the sentiment that seeing people who look like us in the places we aspire to be is important, and this symposium was the first time I had personally encountered female or Latina surgeons in this field.”

Participants also indicated interest in continuing neurosurgical involvement after the symposium. On the postsurvey, 97.6% of participants indicated interest in the longitudinal mentorship program introduced during the symposium. More than 95% of scholars also indicated interest in neurosurgery-based research, with 71% indicating interest in clinical research, 40.3% in global health research, and 30.6% in translational research. Furthermore, 89.5% of participants indicated interest in the Future Neurosurgeons Scholarship sponsored by the Future Neurosurgeons Foundation Inc. Twenty-six students applied for the scholarship, and 4 of those applicants were awarded the scholarship. Supporting information on the symposium impact can be found in Appendix D.

### Attitudes Toward Neurosurgery

Analysis of participant attitudes toward neurosurgery illustrated several key changes (Fig. 3). Students indicated increased self-confidence after FLNSUS 2021, showing significant increases in their agreement with statements such as “I can become a neurosurgeon” and “I am connected to mentors that can help me become a neurosurgeon.” Participants also reported increased exposure to the specialty and understanding of the field. This was evident through significantly increased agreement with the following statements: “I am familiar with the career pathway to become a neurosurgeon” and “I know the day-to-day responsibilities of a neurosurgeon.” Participants also indicated significantly increased exposure to neurosurgeons from diverse backgrounds, as well as a reduction in perceived barriers for minorities in neurosurgery. Of note, participant perceptions of the field as a whole only changed in terms of an increased belief in the capacity of neurosurgeons to improve quality of life and a reduced perception of neurosurgeons as intimidating.

### Stratification of Impact Across UREM Groups

An ANOVA was performed to test whether participant race, ethnicity, gender, sexual orientation, or educational stage had an impact on responses to any individual question. The only instance in which one of these factors impacted participant responses differently for a specific group was for the question, “I will be accepted into medical school.” ANOVA indicated a difference between responses for individuals of different gender identities. This specific difference was interrogated via chi-square test comparing the distribution of male and female students to the expected distribution for this question. No clear difference was found, with the chi-square analysis returning a p value of 0.075. Genders other than male or female were excluded from analysis because all other unique groups had an n = 1.

## Discussion

### Impact of FLNSUS

The FLNSUS increased student self-confidence, provided exposure to the specialty, and reduced perceived barriers to UREMs in neurosurgery. To our knowledge, the FLNSUS was the first virtual neurosurgery-specific symposium to target UREM students. The virtual symposium was cost-effective and accessible to students, so we were granted an unparalleled opportunity to reach students around the world from different backgrounds. The symposium was well received by the students, with more than 83% giving it a ranking of 9 out of 10 or higher. We have demonstrated that the FLNSUS significantly impacted participant attitudes toward neurosurgery, improved their understanding of neurosurgery, reduced feelings of intimidation from neurosurgeons, and increased confidence in their ability to become a neurosurgeon. After the program, participants expressed interest in engaging in future opportunities such as neurosurgical research, longitudinal mentorship programs with residents and neurosurgeons, and financial scholarships.

### Long-Term Goals and Intended Outcomes for the FLNSUS

Studies have demonstrated that mentoring students from underrepresented groups helps to shape their scientific identity,20 leads to greater academic success with higher GPAs,21 and fosters career self-efficacy.22 Hemal et al. determined that longitudinal mentorship programs are one of the most effective initiatives to increase underrepresented minorities in surgical specialties.23 Their review concluded that longitudinal mentorship programs increase the likelihood of minority students applying to surgical residency programs.

We hope to build a longitudinal virtual mentorship program to create more intimate mentee-mentor relationships and facilitate opportunities to participate in research projects. Although a virtual mentorship program may limit students’ ability to participate in in-person clinical shadowing and basic science research opportunities, studies have shown the effectiveness of utilizing an online format.24,25 For instance, students can participate in journal clubs, literature reviews, data analyses, and journal article publications.26 Mentors are still able to influence the personal development and career choice of mentees. Notably, virtual mentoring can also occur through social media, and the Norton et al. study has demonstrated promise in using social media to address gender gaps in neurosurgery.27 This strategy could be utilized to address racial and ethnic gaps in neurosurgery for students of historically excluded groups. Mentorship can be mutually beneficial because mentors feel a greater sense of personal gratification, productivity, and career satisfaction.28

There is a lack of literature demonstrating the impact of a brief intervention like the FLNSUS. However, long-term follow-up is needed to measure the program’s impact on student abilities to pursue research and clinical opportunities. In studies looking at the career trajectory of participants engaged in summer academic enrichment programs ranging from 4 to 8 weeks, measures such as the matriculation rate into medical or graduate school and contribution to the formation of professional interests are meaningfully impacted.22,29 With the next cohort of FLNSUS participants, we will send out 6- and 12-month surveys to identify the short- and long-term influence of the symposium on the students’ ability to seek out research and clinical shadowing, as well as on confidence retention. We plan to send out annual surveys to measure the student matriculation rate into medical or graduate school.

### Recruiting Underrepresented Medical Students Interested in Neurosurgery

There is a misconception that UREM medical students generally pursue medical careers to specialize in primary care. On the contrary, Burkhardt et al. analyzed 5 years of applicants who applied to residencies via the Electronic Residency Application Service and found that UREM students expressed more interest in surgical specialties than non-UREM students on matriculation into medical school.30 However, UREM career interests were more likely to shift from surgical specialties before matriculation to nonsurgical specialties upon graduation. It is known that early exposure, fostered mentorship, and targeted research programs are strategic efforts that will lead to the retention of UREMs interested in surgery.31,32 Research programs like the Black Lives Matter Summer Scholarship33 founded by the University of Miami Department of Neurosurgery and the Ray Charles Foundation Scholars Fund in Neurosurgery34 established by the Cedars-Sinai Department of Neurosurgery are exceptional examples of comprehensive opportunities that provide research experiences paired with clinical shadowing for UREM students.

Although the focus of the FLNSUS was on undergraduate students, a considerable number of medical students demonstrated interest in or attended the program. In 2019, Hanrahan et al. showed the importance of hosting neurosurgery-based conferences with interactive workshops and networking opportunities for medical students.35 There was a marked increase in students who understood neurosurgery demands and increased interest in participating in neurosurgery-related research.

Creating symposiums targeted at UREM medical students may lead to the trends demonstrated through our study, such as increased interest in neurosurgery, improved confidence in the ability to become a neurosurgeon, and better engagement in research and mentorship opportunities. It can address factors that deter medical students from pursuing neurosurgery, such as the competitiveness of the specialty36 and work-life balance.37 The symposium could also provide a chance for students to gain insight into the intellectual challenge and technical skills associated with a career in neurosurgery. Brundage et al. showed that emphasizing positive factors such as intellectual challenge, technical skills, and financial reward can increase the attractiveness of surgical specialties to medical students.38

### Study Limitations

As the first neurosurgery-related symposium for UREM college students, this event and our study had some limitations. For instance, Doctor of Osteopathic Medicine was not included in the presymposium survey as a career option. Students may have selected Doctor of Allopathic Medicine as a default response. There were over 200 students in attendance at the symposium, but only 124 individuals completed both the pre- and postsymposium surveys, which not only decreased the analytical power of assessing the impact of FLNSUS, but could also reflect a selection bias in our results. Also, the postsymposium survey was not shared with students immediately after the program concluded, which could have contributed to the decreased postsymposium response rate. The smaller research sample made it challenging to do a subanalysis for individual trends related to race, ethnicity, gender, and sexual orientation. And although 89.5% of the participants were interested in applying for the Future Neurosurgeons Scholarship, we could not measure the impact of the scholarship because we did not ask questions related to the personal financial statuses of the students. Specifically, we do not know about the percentage of participants with financial challenges in paying for MCAT preparation material or applying for medical school and those who qualify for the Association of American Medical Colleges Fee Assistance Program. Future symposiums will also incorporate community neurosurgeons to serve as panelists and small group leaders so that students will have a diverse array of neurosurgical career perspectives.

## Conclusions

The inaugural FLNSUS empowered, educated, and exposed participants to the lifestyle and tripartite mission of academic neurosurgery. It was the first virtual neurosurgical symposium platform for UREM students in medicine that may serve as a working model for future symposiums to promote diversity in neurosurgery within the United States. The greatest impact of the symposium was seen in student attitudes toward becoming a future neurosurgeon, familiarity with the field, and increased exposure to neurosurgeons from diverse gender, racial, and ethnic backgrounds. By expanding the future classes of neurosurgeons that come from a diverse ethnic and racial background, there may be enhanced cultural humility, patient-centered care, and increased research productivity in neurosurgery.
